event_model_payload.headline: Best Beast Of Reincarnation Skills For The Early Game
event_model_payload.summary:
Throughout Beast of Reincarnation, you'll unlock plenty of skills for Emma and Koo, but in the early game that can be a little overwhelming. You'll first need to decide where to invest your attribute points, as some skills and mods are locked until you upgrade the main skill they're nested beneath.

While there are several viable approaches, we think the best way to approach the early game while you're getting to grips with the mechanics is to focus on increasing Emma's AoE damage while leaning on Koo's support abilities. With that in mind, these are the best Beast of Reincarnation skills to focus on unlocking first:

Emma's Best Skills

Hair

Emma's hair can be used as a weapon as default, which isn't immediately obvious. However, putting her attribute points into Vitality and then using skill points on the Hair category to enhance it means that enemies hit with her hair will receive more damage.

Helm Splitter

This skill is nested in the Hair category, and allows Emma to slam down from a height to damage enemies beneath her. You can enhance it, but keep in mind that you'll need to put attribute points into her Vitality stat, otherwise you won't be able to progress it. Helm Splitter is effective against normal enemies and bosses, meaning that Emma can get high away from the danger, and respond with a slam attack.

Petal Barrage

While in midair, Emma can perform a targeted area attack that deals huge damage. Use this when you're facing bosses, or large groups of enemies, as it'll take down a chunk of their health. Use this time to combine it with an attack from Koo for maximum effect.

Tracking Shot

Although this is another of Emma's base skills, it's worth having, especially if you use ranged weapons often. Hitting an enemy with her ranged weapon will infuse your arrows with blight, so they'll track enemies. You'll need to have 7 attribute points in Emma's Florescence stat, so don't prioritize this over the others, but grab it when you can.

Koo's Best Skills

Pounce

Koo's base Pounce skill requires attribute points to be put into his Strength stat to enhance it, but it's well worth it. When Emma commands Koo to "Run Ahead" he will seek out weak enemies and pounce on them to instantly kill them. The chance of success is shown above the enemy's head, but this can't be used against strong enemies or Nushi.

Detect Hidden Item

Koo's ability to detect hidden items requires the Pounce skill to be level two or above, but it comes in handy when exploring new areas. He'll alert you to unusual objects, seeds, strongboxes, and more.

Dokuzeri: Fang

This attack is obtained after the second boss, but it's worth using as soon as you have it. Koo's fangs will become laced with venom that cause poisonous dokuzeri flowers to bloom. The enemy will also become poisoned, taking damage over time.

Lay Flame Trap / Lay Landmine

You'll need the initial Lay Landmine skill before you can acquire the Lay Flame Trap skill, but these enable Koo to lay dangerous traps for enemies during battle. It's a good way of controlling the field when facing more than one enemy.

With that said, there are plenty of viable combinations especially in the later game, these are just the skills we recommend concentrating on first. Later on, you'll find Emma's ability to link her shots with elemental effects is hugely effective. If you're looking for more helpful hints, check out our Beast of Reincarnation tips.

event_model_payload.headline: Beast Of Reincarnation’s Cinematic Focus Fails Its Flashy Action
event_model_payload.summary:
When you start a new game in Game Freak’s Beast of Reincarnation, a prompt asks if you’d like to play in cinematic mode. This locks the cutscene frame rate to 24 frames per second, but, understandably, leaves the gameplay as is. When I first saw this during my 90-minute preview session last month, it felt like a bold statement from Game Freak. Pokemon, Game Freak’s multigenerational smash-hit, can be described as many things, but cinematic it certainly is not. Unfortunately, aside from its flashy combat and a few cutscenes, Beast of Reincarnation isn't really cinematic, either. Flat performances and robotic animations undermine its fascinating story, bland environments sour its beautiful art direction, and an overall lack of polish hampers its intense combat. Though there are aspects of Beast of Reincarnation that I adored, for each one of them there’s always something that holds it back.

Beast of Reincarnation takes place exactly 2,000 years in the future, in 4026. After civilization was nearly wiped out by a phenomenon called The Blight, an infection that causes humans and animals alike to sprout vegetation, humanity transferred their souls into machines called golems to quell the spread. This inadvertently conquered death, but the relocated souls eventually deteriorated, leaving corrupted golems in their wake. The wildlife didn’t fare much better. Infected beasts called Malefacts wander the ruins of Japan attacking everything and everyone in their path. There’s a captivating history here that weaves together multiple science-fiction subgenres to create an intriguing world. The creatures that wander the wasteland feel biopunk-inspired, the aforementioned golem backstory is pulled from the cyberpunk genre, and the landscapes and architecture would feel at home in solarpunk fiction. Despite its many inspirations, Beast of Reincarnation’s world feels distinct.

This, in part, is due to the art direction. The futuristic technology juxtaposed alongside the overgrown ruins of Japan creates some memorable vistas that reflect the world’s alluring history. Emma, Beast of Reincarnation’s stoic protagonist, represents that fusion of technology and nature succinctly with her design. Her angular monochrome outfit is punctuated by a braid adorned with flowers that grows longer as she becomes stronger. It’s a nice touch that reflects your progress in her character design.

The plot centers around Emma and her dog Koo as they travel across Japan to reach the capital and hunt down the titular Beast of Reincarnation. Emma and Koo’s journey is frequently halted as they’re tasked with taking down a Nushi in each area--powerful Malefacts that spread The Blight. Each of these semi-open areas share a similar structure: You arrive, battle your way through the area, explore a little, and fight the boss. There are optional enemies to dispatch and loot to find, but these locales start to blend together after a while. Most of them consist of open fields with tall, green grass. As you get closer to the capital, those fields will be replaced with dry deserts. There are some interesting nooks hidden around each map, but it feels like a lot of wasted space.

There’s really not much to say about Emma. She’s a vessel, meaning she can absorb the power from enemies she’s defeated, but she is devoid of personality. She’s been told to fight and that’s exactly what she does. There are lore reasons for her languid disposition, but it doesn’t change the fact that nearly every interaction she has falls flat. In one scene, she robotically asks one of her traveling companions what love is. Her companion dryly explains that love is what happens when you miss people. This is made worse by deadpan voice work, static animations, and awkward editing that often leaves seconds of dead air between dialogue. The actors' performances are a little easier to stomach in Japanese, but the characters never escape what's largely dull writing.

This isn’t relegated to a few scenes, either. The entire script lacks subtext and nuance. Frequently, you return to your mobile base of operations, called a Cleanse Walker, to chat with your teammates. A young girl named Kagura who Emma saves early in the story tends to your base by cooking meals and managing resources. She happens to be just as dull as Emma, making their shared conversations painful to witness as the two emotionlessly talk about food or journals. There’s no energy behind their performances, the camera work lacks any creative direction, and they are always confined to the grey walls of the Cleanse Walker.

Ironically, the best character in the game doesn’t talk. Koo, Emma’s canine companion, is fierce and adorable. In one moment he’s lovingly looking up at Emma as they explore the world, and in the next he’s ripping out the titanium throat of a golem. He whimpers, barks, and even collects items for Emma. He’s an endearing companion with some charming animations, but Emma and Koo’s relationship never really develops throughout the game. We get some backstory here and there, but I never felt like they were forging a bond. Emma just doesn’t seem all that interested in Koo for most of the game. In one scene, a character suggests that Emma do something nice for Koo and after some consideration, she suggests petting him. Once again, there are lore reasons for her listlessness, which I won’t spoil, but it doesn’t change the fact that these scenes are so dull.

If there’s anything in Beast of Reincarnation that can be described as “cinematic,” it’s the combat. The parry-heavy skirmishes are fantastic. Enemies are deadly and aggressive, and can cut Emma down in a few hits. While it isn’t nearly as hard as something like From Software’s Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice or Neowiz’s Lies of P, Beast of Reincarnation can be tough–especially if you aren’t using the full range of Emma and Koo’s abilities.

The fundamentals are there. Emma’s slashes feel weighty, the clang of parrying a attack is gratifying, and her lethal blows are vicious. Like Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice, enemies have a health bar and a stagger bar. Deflecting attacks and pressuring enemies will fill up the stagger bar. Once it’s full, Emma can unleash a powerful attack that instantly kills a basic enemy. There is a dodge and a block too, but mastering the parry window is far more rewarding. 

Alongside Emma’s basic attacks, she has unlockable skills that can be deployed mid-combo for dazzling effect. These skills are themed around different blossoms and successfully pulling off one of these moves results in massive flowers blooming on the battlefield. Generally, these combos do significantly more damage than basic attacks, but they require some windup and leave Emma vulnerable. This means you need to study an enemy's patterns to find an opening. Combat, especially later in the game, is a spectacle. Flowers and trees spring up around Emma as she cuts down foes with style.

What separates Beast of Reincarnation’s combat from similar action games is Koo. By pressing Y or Triangle, time stops, and Emma can issue commands. These commands cost FP, which is accumulated by successfully parrying attacks. In order to efficiently take down tougher enemies and bosses, you need to be aggressive with Emma while juggling Koo’s FP and commands. Some of these moves may also synergize with Emma’s skills. For example, Koo has a command that can bind or stun some enemies for a brief period of time, giving Emma just enough time to follow up with one of her powerful combos.

The near-constant stream of new combos, abilities, commands, and weapons kept the combat fresh throughout my entire playthrough. It’s almost a little overwhelming as Emma and Koo’s individual skill trees grow larger and larger throughout the story, but I never felt compelled to unlock everything. Each branch and root within Emma and Koo’s skill trees supports a different playstyle, and part of the fun is mixing and matching these different abilities to fit into your playstyle. While the parry-first combat is at the center of every approach, there are dozens of ancillary strategies that you can lean into. For example, I heavily invested skill points into Emma’s Sakura Blade Art, which happens to be one of the longest combos in the game. Given its windup, I prioritized Koo commands that would bind enemies. Max Blumenthal, a video producer on staff, focused more on Emma’s Kiku Blade Art, which has a much shorter windup and more range. He also invested more heavily in Koo’s commands, finding ways to chain his attacks to great effect. 

This all comes together during boss fights. These special Malefacts, known as Nushi, tower over Emma and Koo. They are based on real-world animals that have been infected by the Blight. Root tendrils hang off of them and giant flowers sprout from their body. They are beautiful and terrifying. Most of these bosses have two phases, and pushed me to conserve resources and tap into both Emma and Koo’s many abilities. There’s an engaging back and forth of reacting to the boss’s attacks and applying pressure whenever you find an opening. Sprinkling in commands from Koo can extend those openings or exploit a weakness. Some bosses are tricky but none felt insurmountable thanks to Emma and Koo’s wide array of skills and commands.

The problem is that most of these bosses are reused in the second half of the game. They are a higher level, but their attack patterns are nearly identical. This makes most of the high stakes encounters in later areas a cake walk. I don’t necessarily mind refighting bosses, but it robs these fights of any tension and opportunity for further experimentation. I know which attacks to counter and when to use one of Emma’s skill arts before the introductory cutscene has finished.

As stylish as the combat is, it lacks the polish of its inspirations. The camera can be unruly, timing perfect dodges feels inconsistent, and Emma’s traversal maneuvers can lead to some awkward situations. Where the camera struggles the most is against large bosses. In order to pressure a Nushi, you need to get in close, but when you’re stuck under their legs, it’s tough to tell when they are swinging and if they will even hit you. Occasionally they’ll fire off an attack that can only be dodged, and if you time your dodge right, time will slow down, allowing you to counter attack. Nailing this timing feels good, but it didn’t always behave consistently. Sometimes I’d dodge well before an attack and it would trigger the slowdown, and other times I would time it right before an attack and I’d still get hit. 

You can also get around enemy attacks with Emma’s hair. By holding the jump button or right trigger, you can extend Emma’s root-like hair to reach new heights and cross gaps. These abilities can be used to close the distance between an enemy, get out of harm's way, or kick off aerial combos and attacks. It’s fun to weave these traversal skills into her moves, but they don’t always work as intended. At times her hair wouldn’t extend all the way, and other times I wouldn’t be able to grapple onto the endpoint to pull her forward. These issues are minor, but they add up and leave the combat feeling messy at times. 

Part of that messiness stems from Beast of Reincarnation’s inconsistent performance and visual bugs. I played a majority of the game on a PC equipped with an RTX 4080, and I noticed some micro-stutters and hitches at 1080p and 1440p. I can’t say how well it fares at higher resolutions, because it wouldn’t let me change resolution settings unless I set it to full screen--a setting that doesn’t seem to exist for me in the current build. Based on our testing, the PlayStation 5 and PlayStation 5 Pro seems to be the best option while the Xbox Series X has severe frame rate issues that Game Freak is aware of and intends to address before its release.

Beast of Reincarnation is an ambitious game that often overextends itself. The lack of polish taints its versatile combat, the mundane performances and wearisome dialogue suffocate its tantalizing story, and the uninteresting areas drag down strong art direction. That isn’t to say Beast of Reincarnation is a total miss, though. The combat, despite my nitpicks, feels and looks great when you’re chaining together combos and deflecting ferocious attacks. And aside from the cutscenes, my 25-hour adventure didn’t feel like a slog--I was eager to improve Emma and Koo’s skills to take down tougher enemies. But everything surrounding that core loop falls flat. Despite Beast of Reincarnation’s enticing mix of high-quality inspirations, it fails to reach the same heights as those experiences.

Beast of Reincarnation is the new action-RPG from Pokemon developer Game Freak, and offers a very different experience from the creature-collecting bliss you're used to. It has three difficulty options, with each being designed so that a wider variety of players can enjoy it, unlike a typical Soulslike game.

Story Mode is best for those who want to play through the narrative without finding combat too challenging. Parry timing is more forgiving, and enemies deal less damage. You'll still need to engage with the combat, but you'll be punished far less for any mistakes you make. If you're playing this for the Game Freak name rather than a passion for a challenging RPG, opt for Story Mode.

Normal Mode is the intended experience, with balanced challenges and normal parry timing. It's intended to encourage you to learn enemy attack patterns, rely on Koo and his abilities, and experiment with your build to find the optimal combinations.

Hard Mode is for those Soulslike fanatics who want a serious challenge. The parry window is alarmingly tight, and you'll be punished for any mistakes you make. If you've mastered the combat system and want to experience the game's full brutality, this is the option for oyu.

However, director Kota Furushima has explained that the game's challenge isn't just determined by the difficulty you play on. By tinkering with Emma and Koo's skill trees, Spirit Stones that modify combat, and different builds, you can find the game easier or harder as you progress through it.

When you're playing, you'll notice that when selecting Koo's Blooming Arts, time slows down to give you the option to think about your approach instead of button mashing and hoping for the best. Make sure to read the skill trees too, as there are many different button combinations for different attacks, and if you're not reading those, you won't be using Emma or Koo to their full potential.

Can you change difficulty in Beast of Reincarnation?

The good news is that yes, you can change difficulty after starting your playthrough of Beast of Reincarnation. This also means that the difficulty option you choose doesn't affect the rewards that you get as you progress. You can choose the option best for you without losing any potentially larger rewards for playing on harder difficulties.

Note that you cannot change the difficulty from the menu unless you have an active session open--so you won't be able to adjust it from the main menu before continuing your game.

If you're struggling on your chosen difficulty, check out our Beast of Reincarnation tips for some helpful pointers.

event_model_payload.headline: 15 Years Ago, Catherine Had Gaming’s Most Complex Trans Representation
event_model_payload.summary:
Catherine celebrated its 15-year anniversary on July 26, 2026. Below, we examine how this game was an early, if awkward, pioneer in trans representation in video games.

When Catherine released in 2011 it was a step outside of the box for developer Atlus. The RPG powerhouse team wasn't as popular as it is today, and while it had built up a solid reputation from developing the Shin Megami Tensei and Persona series, Atlus had yet to quite break through into mainstream gaming. When the team decided to develop Catherine, it did so with the mindset of exploring more adult themes and identities. Chief among them was one of gaming’s few examples of trans representation. Though the intention of this character was well meaning, cultural divides caused a bit of controversy in the West.

After the long development of Shin Megami Tensei: Persona 4, the team decided to branch out into a wildly unexpected direction for its next title. The project would reunite Persona series director and producer Katsura Hashino, character designer Shigenori Soejima, and composer Shoji Meguro, and take them into an entirely new genre of game that allowed for more mature storytelling.

Catherine tells the story of a man named Vincent. Vincent lives a happy life as a bachelor. He has a one-bedroom apartment, goes out drinking with his close friends nearly every night, and has a beautiful girlfriend named Katherine that he’s lagging on marrying. But his life gets upended when he meets the beautiful Catherine, a woman who is temptation made flesh. Soon after their encounter, he is haunted by nightmares every night in his sleep.

The gameplay takes the form of controlling Vincent in his day-to-day life, making decisions in his relationships. This feels like a natural progression of Persona’s school and social systems. But the real bulk of the gameplay happens when Vincent goes to sleep and he’s besieged by nightmares that force him to climb an ever-falling tower of blocks in a puzzle-game fashion. It’s a great inverse of the Persona series--in that series, the gameplay ends at night, and in this one, that's when the bulk of the gameplay begins.

Breaking away from the high school setting of the Persona series allowed the team to tackle more mature themes of infidelity, alcoholism, marriage, and adulthood. It also allowed the team to depict characters that you wouldn't typically see in a high-school-set game such as Persona.

Vincent goes to the bar each night to drink with his friends and decompress after the nightmare from the previous night. This allows players to progress the story and get some opinions from his friends that they can use to influence their future choices, or just get drunk and listen to some good music on the in-game jukebox.

One of the characters at the bar is a waitress named Erica. Featuring a very feminine design, she acts as the one female voice in the game that remains a neutral point to Vincent’s problems, often lending an ear to him and his friends in a flirty manner and providing a point of respite in an emotionally draining situation. Yet the game hints at her harboring a secret--something that was taboo in video games at the time.

Erica is transgender.

The game doesn’t go about this reveal in a tactful manner, though. Over the course of the game, Vincent’s friends begin having the same nightmares as he does. Erica chalks it up to a woman's wrath curse, but when she strikes up a romantic relationship with Vincent’s friend Toby, she begins to have the same nightmares: nightmares that only men have. In addition to this clue, there’s subtle hints dropped throughout the game, but the reveal doesn’t fully happen until the “Katherine True” ending of the game. In this ending of the game, Toby discovers Erica’s true past and the game even refers to her as her deadname (her former name).

This portrayal is problematic for a myriad of reasons to Western culture, but is exemplified in the “Full Body” version of the game, which features a detransitioned Erica in flashbacks and in one of the endings of the game.

While Catherine doesn’t attempt to portray Erica in a malicious manner, the cultural divide between Eastern and Western cultures and their acceptance of trans people is on full display. Japanese culture views gender and sexuality through a wide and varied spectrum that results in various forms of gender expression. For example, in the West when someone is transgender, it is socially expected of them to go through medical and physical transition in order to “pass” through society. Sure, drag subculture is a thing for non-trans people to gender-express, but this isn’t always tied to personal identity.

This is not the case in Japan, as gender expression often results in crossdressing communities or those who do not decide to medically or physically transition. To them, dressing and presenting as female will suffice. In fact, this could be a result of a law passed in 2003 that will allow a trans person to get a legal gender change only if they pass the hurdles of being unmarried, over the age of 22, undergo gender-reassignment surgery, and have no minor children. One cannot even have gender reassignment surgery if they’re on hormone replacement therapy.

This results in Japan’s transgender subculture being more fluid. Perhaps that’s why Erica’s portrayal in Catherine relates so much to her past and not who she is in the moment. While she’s accepted by those around her, in-game it comes with a caveat. In Western culture, perhaps she would be portrayed as her true self with no regard to her past and only looking to the future.

That’s what makes Catherine such a complex game. It’s a game that tackles adult themes and issues but never makes light of them. It’s a look into Japanese social culture and how it differs from the West. It’s a game that’s well meaning and never feels malicious despite arguably problematic elements, and it allowed Atlus to venture into uncharted territory.

event_model_payload.headline: Splatoon Raiders Owes A Lot To Older Campaigns You Forgot About
event_model_payload.summary:
Praise for something new can often come at the expense of what came before it. One aspect of art and media criticism that I find irksome is that to uplift new works, older ones from the same lineage are often undersold at best, or completely thrown under the bus at worst. It’s a trend I’ve seen most recently with Splatoon Raiders, the first spin-off title in one of my favorite Nintendo franchises.

Splatoon Raiders may very well be the best single-player-focused experience in the series, but let’s not fool ourselves into thinking that the campaigns in Splatoons 1, 2, or 3 were significantly inferior, from either a gameplay or story aspect. In fact, they were pretty damn fresh.

Conventional wisdom is that the older Splatoon campaigns are the least memorable aspect of their respective games--in short, they’re extended tutorials that are light on story, and Splatoon Raiders is the most successful story campaign in the series. Each of these points might be true to some degree, but that doesn’t stop the story modes of the original three games from being fun in their own respect.

Splatoon’s single-player stories are short and sweet, infused with Nintendo’s signature charm. Despite their length, these campaigns greatly expand on the franchise’s world and are dripping with fascinating lore (as well as ink, of course). Many of the levels are amusing ways to learn about a range of Splatoon weapons, with clever level-specific gimmicks for players to wrap their heads around in a way that invokes other Nintendo games. And the structure of these story modes are always changing from game to game, experimenting with the very format of how players move between levels. Unpredictability is the format of Splatoon, and each of these older campaigns fed into the foundation that Splatoon Raiders is built on.

The first Splatoon’s Octo Valley campaign did some heavy lifting when it came to fleshing out the Splatoon universe. Establishing Octarians as the antagonistic force and detailing the extensive history between them and the Inklings, with hidden Sunken Scroll collectibles describing an ancient war between the factions with colorful and comprehensive visuals. These scrolls even go the extra mile to answer the sickest questions from players about Inkling evolution and biology.

The levels themselves were like quick bites, carrying the same spirit that other Nintendo titles like Super Mario Galaxy and 3D World have, centering entire levels on mechanics like inkrails and propeller-powered platforms. In short, variety is of no short supply in classic Splatoon campaigns. And through music, Splatoon campaigns differentiated themselves with energetic, quirky, and straight-up disorienting tunes that reflect the contrasts between Inkling and Octarian culture.

Splatoon 2’s Octo Canyon was a solid continuation, keeping the same level structure as Octo Valley while gradually giving players more weapon options to experiment with, letting them take different approaches to the same levels. While the story has an inherently similar premise to the first game, it adds a novel narrative layer by taking the results of the final Splatfest of Splatoon 1 into account, meaning that players’ actions from the previous game actually affected this story.

The Octo Expansion DLC took Splatoon story modes to a completely new height, shifting to a challenge-room-based structure and allowing players to tackle levels in different orders based on a subway map. A favorite of Splatoon fans, Octo Expansion might be the most influential campaign within the series. And as a bonus, it contains one of the hardest gaming bosses of all time--Inner Agent 3--who I think deserves to be named alongside any of the grueling opponents seen in a From Software game.

Splatoon 3’s Return of the Mammalians begins with what seems to be a retread of Octo Valley and Octo Canyon, even throwing the final boss from the first two games at you very early on. But it then switches to a level structure similar to Octo Expansion, with non-linear progression and a ton of unique levels testing your skills with the multiplayer’s special abilities. And Splatoon 3’s Side Order DLC successfully took elements from Octo Expansion, throwing players into intricate challenge rooms and allowing for numerous upgrade and loadout possibilities. What resulted was a uniquely Nintendo roguelite, and a very strong entry in the larger genre.

Although these campaigns weren’t the main focus for their respective games, they were far from throwaways, and Raiders draws from all of these games in one way or another. On the surface, I’ve noticed the focus of lore and history disseminated through hidden scrolls coming from Splatoon 1, while Raiders allows for the weapon versatility and experimentation seen in Splatoon 2. Octo Expansion’s non-linear nature of level progression echoes in Raiders, while Splatoon 3’s ability tutorials show through Raiders’ Sampler Dungeons. Even the spec-building systems in Raiders certainly resemble the permanent upgrade system seen in Side Order.

You can view Splatoon Raiders as a culmination of ideas from the franchise’s decade-plus history: a refinement of the elements from campaigns past into a solid standalone experience. But that isn’t to diminish any titles in the series compared to the others, because they all brought something of their own. Heck, Raiders is my least favorite one, since PvP is why I go to Splatoon--but it’s still a damn good game. 

Everyone will have their preference and favor one over the rest, but if there’s one takeaway from Raiders, it’s not that what preceded it was worse, but that Splatoon as a whole is something truly special.

event_model_payload.headline: Halo: Campaign Evolved Reminded Me That Halo Infinite Was Great, Actually
event_model_payload.summary:
Halo: Combat Evolved is 25 years old now, so it's a marvel that playing its most recent remake, Halo: Campaign Evolved, is still as fun as it is. Everything from the weight of the weaponry, the ambiance of the Halo installation, the screams of fleeing grunts, and the grin-inducing sound of a plasma grenade exploding on an unfortunate target are all here to remind you (or introduce you) to the most important franchise in Xbox history. It's a series that has struggled in recent times, and it's easy to see this reminder of Halo's roots as critical to its future. So why do I keep wanting to go back to its flawed, latest entry instead?

Halo Infinite was always going to miss the mark in some way. It was a victim of troubled development, responsible for selling a console that struggled out of the gate, and tasked with being both an end to the tired tale from previous entries as well as the start of a wholly new one. Infinite was pitched as Halo's future; a platform that could be built upon for years to come, telling an evolving tale as new chapters were added to it over a decade or more. None of that came to pass. Halo Infinite did a lot of things, but it wasn't enough to pull the series out of the ditch it found itself in. So instead of committing to it long-term, 343 Industries reformed into Halo Studios, shut down its in-house Slipspace engine in favor of the ubiquitous Unreal Engine 5, and did what was once unthinkable: It brought Master Chief to PlayStation.

Yet none of that should overshadow just how much Halo Infinite did to drive forward the fundamental gameplay loop that made its original so captivating in 2001. Halo: Combat Evolved has an incredibly strong opening, thrusting you into the chaos of its intergalactic war and wasting no time introducing you to its striking setting on the surface of the Halo installation. Having wide-open areas to explore as enemies drop in from the horizon was as novel then as it is today. It's a little easier to pick apart the loop--drive to a spot in the world, survive a few waves of enemies, move on and do it again--especially in those opening sections. But it's a rhythm that Combat Evolved, and by extension Campaign Evolved, uses to great effect across its brief adventure, at least by today's standards.

Halo Infinite took this idea, one that had been mostly abandoned since Halo 3, and completely modernised it. You're on yet another installation, but this time the map isn't just wide--it's open. Enemies are littered around its landscapes, occupying fortified bases for you to break into, suppressing small squads of lost UNSC soldiers, and patrolling the valleys with vehicles just waiting to be hijacked. You were finally given the freedom to explore and engage with the world in a way that was only simulated in previous games, letting you approach skirmishes in the ways that you saw fit with new weapons and tools that encouraged creativity. 

The hookshot, Infinite's version of a wrist-mounted grappling hook, was smartly given to you from the start. It's Infinite's single best addition to its combat loop, letting you move in a way that made Master Chief an even greater force to be reckoned with. Reeling yourself into enemies to deliver that crunching, final melee blow, pulling explosives towards you so that you could fling them into a group of unsuspecting enemies, and throwing yourself around corners and into the air for a surprise attack are just a few examples of how this tool added new layers to the two-decades-old formula that had strayed too far from its roots. It stripped things back to the fundamentals and accentuated them rather than trying to replace them with gimmicky, hero-like abilities that felt at odds with the shooter they were attempting to integrate with.

Halo Infinite was not without its flaws. Its opening is drawn out and takes too long to unleash you into its open world. The larger, explorable space comes at the expense of the varied locales previous games allowed you to hop between, begging for the variety that chapters like The Silent Cartographer, set against sandy beaches and towering cliff faces, are so fondly remembered for. Its story is almost incomprehensible if you hadn't kept up with the narrative beats conveyed through other expanded-universe Halo media that takes place after the events of Halo 5, particularly regarding what happened to Cortana. It muddies its many gameplay enhancements behind a game that was disinterested with new fans, despite its requirement to act as a platform for its immediate future.

It's easy to see why, then, that Halo Studios saw fit to start over--to remind people why Halo was important, what its core fundamentals are, and reestablish a new future. But it would be a massive shame if this comes at the expense of the first real refinement that this original formula received just a handful of years ago. Halo Infinite is flawed, but it's also the most interesting campaign the series has delivered since the culmination of the Master Chief's initial story under the stewardship of Bungie. And if Halo Studios seeks to reclaim some of the glory of those days, it needs to take lessons from both its recent and distant past.

event_model_payload.headline: Riftbound’s Card Templates Are Getting A Big Overhaul in 2027
event_model_payload.summary:
Riftbound, Riot Games' League of Legends trading card game (TCG), recently celebrated its one-year anniversary on August 1 during GenCon. Since its launch late last year, the game's undergone dozens of changes, errata, rules updates, and even card bans. In its first of three State of the Game updates this week (and second overall this year), Riot broke down some of the biggest changes coming to Riftbound starting in January of 2027 with the release of the game's sixth set, Legacy.

Two State of the Game update articles were released today on Riot's site. One was an in-depth conversation with Riftbound brass Dave Guskin, Chengran Chai, and Nik Davidson, penned by the game's Editor-in-Chief Trick Jarrett, in which they discussed how they felt about the game one year in, and some of the biggest learnings the team has experienced in that time.

Regarding banning cards, Riftbound Game Director Dave Guskin explained that the team doesn't set out to ban cards, but will when absolutely necessary, citing the powerful "Miracle" package from Spiritforged. "I don’t regret making powerful things," he said. "We want you all to have cool stuff to experiment with! But as we learn the nuances of making Riftbound (which is something we are doing right alongside you all, our extremely intelligent players) we’ve learned there’s still room to grow in how we approach designing the six domains and gauging the true power of certain game mechanics."

Last week's release of Riftbound's fourth set, Vendetta, brought along three preemptive bans in an effort for the team to get ahead of the set's release and ensure it has a healthy competitive meta on day one. The team also confirmed that they will continue to monitor powerful strategies and infinite combos going forward.

The other article detailed new products still to come in 2026, and offered a glimpse at the first half of 2027's set releases. What's most interesting from this article is Riot's breakdown of some big changes coming when Legacy launches on January 29. A few of these changes have been desired by the community for months (myself included), and Riot is making it a priority to listen to players and build the game with them. Riftbound will "continue to be reactive to player feedback as it grows," the article read. Guskin went on to explain that the team "will always try to clearly communicate as we improve our process and learn lessons we apply to the game in the future. Building this game together with the community is vitally important to us".

One of the biggest changes coming to the TCG affects booster pack contents. Usually, packs of Riftbound contain 14 cards; seven commons, three uncommons, two rare or higher cards, a foil card of any rarity, and a token or Rune. Legend cards, which are required to build your decks and play the game, have occupied a Rare slot since launch. Riot has said in the past that their goal is to make these cards very easy to come by, and that's been the case, but occupying the Rare slot means players miss out on more, actual rare (read: hard to find) cards. Starting with Legacy, Legend cards will be taking up a common slot, leaving room for the promised two rare or better cards, and bringing the amount of commons in a pack from seven to six.

The next big change has to do with the card templates and text itself, offering a clearer explanation of how cards and how they resolve. Also starting with Legacy, Riftbound will be introducing an arrow icon to signify the effect a triggered ability has.

Next, cards with specific targets will have that word set to a gray background to make sure it's obvious which word on the card is the intended target of a spell or ability.

Finally, one of the biggest changes is all about what the term "play" actually means. Since the game came out, "play" has always referred to making a token appear, placing a card on the chain, finalizing a spell, or resolving an ability. The article explains that these aren't exhaustive enough, so changes are being made to clarify that definition of "play." To start, finalizing a spell or playing a card from your trash pile is unchanged. But moving forward, cards that make tokens will swap "play" out with "create," and cards that say "when you play me" will be changed to "when I enter," meaning their effects are triggered when they resolve in play.

Today's articles kick off the first of three days of Riftbound's State of the Game updates, so expect more news and announcements throughout the week.

event_model_payload.headline: No Matter Which You Choose, Graphics Cards Are About To Get A Lot More Expensive
event_model_payload.summary:
Hold on tight to the graphics cards you have, because those sitting on retailer shelves are about to get a lot more expensive, irrespective of whether you prefer AMD or Nvidia.

Last week, Nvidia GPUs were confirmed to be getting a substantial price hike, with anything between 20% and 30% being reported. That gave AMD the perfect moment to communicate a price increase of its own, with market analyst Harukaze571 reporting that the company had been waiting for Nvidia to make the first move.

The report, via PC Gamer, suggests that AMD was planning its own GPU price hike, but was worried about its effect on current stock, the price sensitivity of consumers, and more. Unlike Nvidia, however, AMD's increase seems mild by comparison, with the company aiming for "at least 10%" but falling short of specifying an upper limit.  Harukaze5719 added that, "price positioning is expected to be similar to that of the Nvidia series graphics cards," with the increases set to start taking place this week.

This increases are, notably, applying to partners, who then have to figure out how much to pass onto consumers. But given the thin margins that GPUs are currently sold at, it is unlikely that many, if any, will be able to absorb any part of the cost.

The increases across the board are attributed to the ongoing demand for memory, which is a core component for GPUs that requires large quantities of high speed modules. Samsung, which supplies a lot of memory for applications including and beyond GPUs, has already increased prices this year, and plans to hike them by a further 20% this month too. The company is expected to continue doing so until 2028 at the earliest.

These are all causing massive knock-on effects across the industry. The Xbox Series X and Series S had its new, increased prices go into effect at the start of the month, with Nintendo soon to follow with its announced Switch 2 price hike. Sony was forced to increase the price of the PlayStation 5 earlier this year, with all three companies likely looking at the possibility of further increases in the further should memory prices continue rising.

event_model_payload.headline: Baldur’s Gate 3 Third-Person Mod Revitalizes The Game
event_model_payload.summary:
When Baldur's Gate 3 launched in 2023, it didn't take long for modders to add new camera options, including a third-person view. Now, a new third-person mod is expanding the view of Baldur's Gate 3 and allowing veteran players a chance to revisit the game from a fresh perspective.

The true third-person mod was created and posted by Nexus mods user Relysia, who acknowledges that it builds upon the previously released native camera tweeks mod and retains its features. However, the new mod adds a way to toggle between an over-the-shoulder camera view and the normal view. Relysia also shared a video comparison between the earlier mod and the current one, as well as a broad overview of its features and options.

As originally used in the game, the camera was locked and didn't allow players to look up or down when using close view. The true third-person camera mod offers more leeway for players to move the camera with the touch of a button. It also keeps the camera "locked tight on your character" and adjusts the FOV when the player is running or crouching while also accounting for different heights for each character.

During combat and turn-based sequences, the mod auto-switches to distant view before reverting to close view. Relysia notes that the mod works best with a controller, but it can also be used with a keyboard. There are some known issues and bugs that remain to be worked out, but the "fix stuck camera" button should be able to help players out if they find themselves trapped in a bad camera angle.

Last year, a group of modders announced their plan to recreate the original Baldur's Gate in Baldur's Gate 3. Remakes of Baldur's Gate and Baldur's Gate 2 are rumored to be in the works, but they have yet to be confirmed by Wizards of the Coast. A Baldur's Gate TV series is also in development, but Baldur's Gate 4 may have more trouble coming to fruition. At least one developer passed on Baldur's Gate 4 after expressing a desire to avoid following up on the work created by Larian Studios.

event_model_payload.headline: Inviting beaches and delightful physics await you in literal sandbox game, Sandcastle
event_model_payload.summary:

event_model_payload.headline: Two years on from taking the role, Wizards of the Coast's president is stepping down
event_model_payload.summary:
Wizards of the Coast president John Hight is stepping down from the role. As reported by GamesIndustry.biz, a US Securities and Exchange Commission filing from July 27th revealed that Hight will be moving on from the role come September 1st. This doesn't mean he's leaving the company completely, as he'll be shifting into an advisor role. The change in role comes roughly two years after Hight took it in August 2024, and after WOTC owner Hasbro took a $56 million impairment charge last week.
